subtitle: Ancient Etruscan Divination Artifact
intro: A bronze model from the late 2nd to early 1st century BCE, mapping the cosmological structure of Etruscan religious beliefs through {totalInscriptions} inscriptions across {totalZones} divine zones.

historicalDiscovery.heading: Historical Discovery
historicalDiscovery.content: The Piacenza Liver was discovered in 1877 near Gossolengo, just outside Piacenza, Italy. This remarkable bronze artifact dates to the late 2nd to early 1st century BCE, making it one of the most significant surviving documents of Etruscan religious practice. The liver model appears to preserve a cosmological teaching map, inscribed with deity names and divine regions. It is cited in Etruscan epigraphic corpora as ET Pa 4.2 (Rix, Etruskische Texte) and TLE 719 in the numbered Testimonia Linguae Etruscae corpus.

hepatoscopy.heading: Hepatoscopy
hepatoscopy.content: Hepatoscopy, or haruspicy, was the ancient Etruscan practice of divination through the examination of animal livers. Priests known as haruspices would sacrifice animals and carefully study the liver's shape, color, texture, and any unusual markings. Sections of the liver could be interpreted through associations with deities or cosmic regions, allowing priests to reason about omens and divine will. This practice was so central to Etruscan religion that it influenced Roman religious traditions for centuries.

liverStructure.heading: The Liver Structure
liverStructure.content: On the visceral (inferior) surface, three prominent anatomical protrusions serve as fixed reference points for interpretation: the processus papillaris, the gall bladder, and the processus pyramidalis. The papillary and pyramidal processes are genuine parts of a real sheep's liver, and their size or shape could vary in sacrificial animals, making them especially meaningful in divinatory reading. Between them lies the gall bladder, shown as a distinct sac-like bulge and treated as a particularly charged feature where strong or unstable forces could be signaled.

cosmologicalStructure.heading: Cosmological Structure
cosmologicalStructure.content: This visualization divides the liver into {totalZones} cosmological zones used for navigation and interpretation. The Sky and Water zones gather celestial, atmospheric, and aquatic powers; the Earth and Underworld zones gather terrestrial and chthonic names; Pars Familiaris and Pars Hostilis mark favorable and unfavorable orientations in the interpretive tradition. The Gall Bladder, Central Section, and Back preserve additional anatomical and celestial reference points.

etruscanPantheon.heading: The Etruscan Pantheon
etruscanPantheon.content: The {totalInscriptions} inscriptions currently map to {totalDeities} deity labels in this dataset. Some identifications are secure: Tinia is compared with Zeus and Jupiter, Nethuns with Poseidon and Neptune, Fufluns with Dionysus and Bacchus, and Hercle with Herakles and Hercules. Others, including Thufltha, Cilens, Lethams, Catha, Lusal, and Tluscva, are treated here as debated or obscure. Each placement is best read as an interpretive map of the liver, not as a complete translation of every inscription.

editorialMethod.heading: Editorial Method
editorialMethod.content: This project is an interpretive visualization, not a full epigraphic edition. Three independent dimensions of evidence are tracked. Reading distinguishes a clearly legible inscription, difficult reading owing mainly to corrosion or wear on the bronze (“unclear”), and forms that are visibly engraved but disputed in strokes or division among scholars (“debated”). Identification marks how secure the modern Etruscan deity identification is, on a four-tier scale (secure, probable, debated, unresolved). Each Greek or Roman parallel carries its own status (secure, proposed, or superseded), so that older equivalences such as Satres / Saturn are preserved as scholarship history rather than silently dropped. Per-deity sources are listed in author-date short form and link to the cited works where openly available. The modern foundation rests on Colonna 1991 (Studi Etruschi LIX) for interpreting the inscribed deities alongside Maggiani 1982 (Studi Etruschi L) and van der Meer 1987 (the only book-length synthesis of the artifact); cosmological discussion draws on Stevens 2009, Pernigotti 2018, and Gottarelli 2018; wider synthesis on Krauskopf 2013 and Maras 2017. Transliterations follow Rix, Etruskische Texte (1991), with corrections from Maggiani 1982 where noted.

significanceAndInterpretation.heading: Significance and Interpretation
significanceAndInterpretation.content: As one of the few surviving Etruscan religious artifacts with extensive inscriptions, the Piacenza Liver provides invaluable insight into a civilization whose written records are largely lost. The artifact demonstrates the sophistication of Etruscan religious thought and their systematic approach to divination, serving as a bridge between Etruscan, Greek, and Roman religious practices. Modern scholarship draws on Adriano Maggiani's foundational epigraphic analysis (1982) and Antonio Gottarelli's cosmological interpretation, which organize the inscriptions into coherent theological groups. This framework reveals how the Etruscans understood the relationship between divine forces, natural phenomena, and human affairs. The liver model was likely used as a teaching tool for apprentice haruspices.

dualSkySystem.heading: Two Celestial Systems
dualSkySystem.content: Recent studies by Antonio Paolo Pernigotti (2018) have proposed that the Etruscans used two different systems for dividing the sky. The first, linked to the diurnal motion of the sun and based on cardinal axes, was used for observing and interpreting lightning (ars fulguratoria), dividing the sky into sixteen equal parts. The second, linked to the annual motion of the sun and based on solstitial axes, defined the celestial dwellings of the deities. According to this interpretation, the sixteen cells on the liver's outer rim are not oriented according to cardinal points, but rather according to the sunrise and sunset positions at the solstices.

technicalDetails.heading: Technical Details
technicalDetails.content: The bronze model measures approximately 12.6 cm in length and 7.6 cm in width, accurately representing the proportions of an actual sheep liver. The inscriptions are written in the Etruscan alphabet, which was derived from the Greek alphabet but adapted for the Etruscan language. Each inscription marks a specific anatomical region, creating a precise map that would have been memorized by practicing haruspices.

howToCite.heading: How to cite this site
howToCite.format: Andraghetti, L. ({year}). The Piacenza Liver: an interactive scholarly visualization. https://piacenzaliver.com/
howToCite.sigla: The artifact itself is catalogued as ET Pa 4.2 in Rix's Etruskische Texte (1991) and as TLE 719 in the Testimonia Linguae Etruscae numbering. Use those sigla when referring to the bronze model rather than to this website.
